sections.h2: What are the ways to sell a house in Knoxville, TN?
sections.html:
You can list the house with an agent, sell it yourself, or take a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. Each route trades speed against price and effort, and which one fits depends on the condition of the house and how soon you need to be done.

Knoxville is a city of 202,021 people as of July 1, 2025, according to Census QuickFacts, up 6.0% from the 2020 base. Only 46.6% of housing units are owner-occupied, so a large share of the stock is rental property, and the median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020-2024 is $239,700. Those two numbers explain why landlords and heirs with an extra house are common sellers here.

  • Listing with an agent: widest exposure, but you pay for showings, repairs a buyer's inspector flags, and months of carrying costs.
  • Selling on your own: you keep the commission, and you also handle the contract, the deed and the closing paperwork.
  • A cash offer: fewer showings and a closing date you pick, usually at a lower price than a repaired and staged listing would reach.

sections.h2: What should a Knoxville seller know about the city and its neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Knoxville sits on the Tennessee River in the Great Appalachian Valley, and the city covers about 104 square miles, according to Wikipedia. Buyers and renters think in terms of five parts of town, and each draws a different kind of house.

  • Downtown and the Old City: mixed residential and commercial blocks around Gay Street, close to the University of Tennessee campus and Fort Sanders.
  • South Knoxville: south of the river, including Vestal, Island Home Park and Colonial Hills, with Chapman Highway and Alcoa Highway as the main corridors.
  • West Knoxville: Sequoyah Hills, Bearden, Cedar Bluff and the Kingston Pike area, near West Town Mall and Turkey Creek.
  • East Knoxville: Parkridge, Burlington, Morningside and Five Points along Magnolia Avenue.
  • North Knoxville: Fountain City and Inskip-Norwood, with Broadway as the commercial spine.

Interstates 40 and 75 meet west of downtown, I-640 loops the north side, and I-140 (Pellissippi Parkway) links West Knoxville to McGhee Tyson Airport and Maryville. The Census Bureau lists a mean commute of 20.2 minutes, which is short for a metro of nearly 958,000 people.

sections.h2: Does Knoxville's climate and terrain affect what a house is worth?
sections.html:
It can, mainly through summer heat, steady rain and sloping lots. Knoxville has a humid subtropical climate with about 36 days a year at 90 degrees or higher, annual precipitation just under 52 inches and roughly 4.6 inches of snow in a normal winter, per the same Wikipedia entry.

Ridges and hills such as Sharp's Ridge, Brown Mountain and Beaver Ridge mean many lots slope, and creeks like First, Second and Third Creek run through the older parts of the city. A buyer's inspector will look at drainage, crawl-space moisture, roof age and the air conditioning system first. Fixing those before a listing costs money and time, which is one reason owners of dated houses consider an as-is sale.

sections.h2: How do city and county property taxes work when you sell in Knoxville?
sections.html:
A Knoxville house is taxed twice, once by the City of Knoxville and once by Knox County, and the unpaid balance on either bill travels with the property to the next owner. The city's property tax page says plainly that a seller's promise to pay does not change what the city can collect from the new owner.

Knoxville property tax facts (City of Knoxville Revenue Office and Knox County Property Assessor)
ItemWhat the offices state
City bill dueOctober 1
City delinquencyMarch 1, with penalty and interest of one percent each per month
City early-payment discount1% on real estate if paid before October 31
Residential assessment ratio25% of appraised value
Commercial assessment ratio40% of appraised value
Reappraisal cycleEvery two years
AppealsCounty Board of Equalization, which meets in June

The assessor, not the city, sets values, and you can reach that office at 865-215-2360. The city revenue office at 865-215-2084 can issue a bill for a property when a buyer needs one. At a closing, the title company normally prorates the year between buyer and seller, so ask for the proration worksheet before you sign.

sections.h2: Can an owner of a Knoxville short-term rental sell the house?
sections.html:
Yes, but the permit does not pass to the buyer by default, so the buyer has to apply for their own. The City of Knoxville requires a permit for any rental of under 30 days, and its short-term rental ordinance took effect in January 2018, as described on the city's short-term rental page.

  • Type 1 permits cover owner-occupied homes in residential areas.
  • Type 2 permits cover non-owner-occupied units in non-residential areas.
  • Applications and annual renewals go through the Business Tax Office.
  • The city contracts with Host Compliance to match online listings against permits, and unpermitted owners can be cited.

If you are selling an unpermitted rental, clear up the citation question with the Business Tax Office first. A complaint hotline runs around the clock at 865-337-8275, so neighbors do report problem units.

sections.h2: What permits and records matter before a Knoxville sale?
sections.html:
Open or missing building permits are the records most likely to slow a closing. The City of Knoxville handles permits through its Plans Review and Inspections online portal, with separate tracks for single-family and townhouse work, mechanical, electrical and plumbing work, and home occupations.

The Knox County Property Assessor says it reviews a property every other year and also checks on permit progress, so a remodel or addition can change the appraised value. The assessor can also arrange a field review if you added a room and want the record to match the house. After a sale, the assessor's office says transfers show up in its system about a week after the deed is recorded, and the state requires a sales questionnaire whenever ownership changes.

sections.h2: How does recording a deed work at the Knox County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
The deed goes to the Register of Deeds in Suite 225 of the City County Building at 400 Main Street, and it is usually recorded the same day it arrives. The Register's FAQ says signatures must be notarized or witnessed by two people, and that there is no deadline for recording, though delay invites legal problems.

The state's realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of the purchase price, per the Tennessee Department of Revenue. On a $240,000 sale that tax comes to $888. The Register's office only records documents. It cannot draft a deed or give legal advice, and a lost deed can be replaced with a certified copy at $1.00 a page. Knox County also offers a free fraud notification system that emails you when a document is recorded under your name.

sections.h2: What tax help exists for older or disabled Knoxville homeowners?
sections.html:
Knox County Trustee runs two programs for owners who live in the house, and approval is by yearly application. For 2026, the Trustee's page lists the following figures.

  • Tax relief for elderly or disabled homeowners: a state-funded credit of up to $85, with a combined 2025 income limit of $38,470.
  • Relief for disabled veterans and their widows or widowers: up to $444, with no income limit.
  • Senior tax freeze: for owners 65 or older, income limit $63,470, covering one home and up to five acres.

Tax relief is a payment credit, not an exemption, so you still receive the bill. If you are selling mid-year, ask the Trustee how the credit is handled before closing.

faqs.q: Do I have to make repairs before selling my Knoxville house?
faqs.a: No. Tennessee does not require repairs before a sale, but lenders and buyer inspections often do. A cash buyer purchases the house in its current condition, so the repair list becomes part of the price instead of your to-do list.

faqs.q: Who pays property tax when a Knoxville house sells?
faqs.a: Both the buyer and seller share the year, usually prorated at closing, but the lien stays with the property. The City of Knoxville states that any unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation whatever the sale contract says, so clear old balances first.

faqs.q: How fast can a Knoxville sale close?
faqs.a: A cash sale can close in days if title is clean, while a financed sale typically takes longer because of appraisal and underwriting. The deed is generally recorded the same day it reaches the Knox County Register of Deeds.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house I inherited in Knoxville?
faqs.a: Yes, once the person with legal authority over the estate can sign the deed. Check the probate status and get certified copies of the court papers, because the title company will ask for them. The Register of Deeds notes that a deed alone does not prove who owns the house, so recorded documents matter.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record the deed in Knox County?
faqs.a: The recording fee is set by Tennessee statute, and the state realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of the price. The Register of Deeds office can tell you the exact recording fee for your document before you file.
